code.title: How call-site decides this

followUps:
It is decided at call time. The same function can give different this values on different calls, because this is a hidden argument filled in by whoever calls it.

Example: function f(){ return this.n } gives 1 for {n:1,f}.f() and 2 for f.call({n:2}). Writing the function inside an object does not fix its this.

The arrow function: it has no own this, so it uses the one from the code around where it was written. That makes it a definition-time (lexical) choice, and no call-site can change it.

Example: inside a method, list.map(x => this.k + x) sees the method's this. A normal function there would get undefined (strict) instead. Class and module code is strict by default.

code.title: Binding rule precedence

followUps:
Build a bound function, then call it with new; the bound object is ignored.

function T(v){ this.v = v; }
const B = T.bind({v: 'bound'}, 'arg');
const o = new B();
console.log(o.v);       // 'arg', not 'bound'
console.log(o instanceof T); // true

The new object came from T.prototype, and only the pre-filled argument survived.

Arrows sit outside the ladder because they never receive a this to bind. The four rules only apply when a function gets its own this, and an arrow does not.

So arrow.call(x), arrow.bind(x)() and obj.arrow() all use the enclosing this; the extra argument is silently ignored. Using new on one throws a TypeError.

You get x. A bound function keeps its [[BoundThis]] forever, so the later .call(y) is ignored.

function f(){ return this.id; }
const g = f.bind({id: 'x'});
g.call({id: 'y'});   // 'x'
g.bind({id: 'z'})(); // still 'x'

Only new g() escapes the lock, and then this is a fresh object.

code.title: call, apply and bind

followUps:
Use apply when the arguments already sit in an array that you cannot spread, or when you want Reflect.apply safety. Spread (f(...arr)) handles most cases now.

Examples: Reflect.apply(Math.max, null, nums) works even if Math.max.apply was overwritten. Old code also used Array.prototype.push.apply(a, b) to append a whole array. Very large arrays (about 100,000+ items) can overflow the argument limit with either form.

bound.name is "bound " plus the original name, and bound.length is the original parameter count minus the pre-filled arguments, never below 0.

function add(a, b, c){}
const f = add.bind(null, 1);
f.name;   // 'bound add'
f.length; // 2

Tools that read length (currying helpers, some frameworks) depend on this being right.

Because every call to bind creates a brand new function object, so a child that compares props by identity sees a change on every render and re-renders for nothing.

Example: onClick={this.handle.bind(this)} in a list of 1,000 rows creates 1,000 new functions per render, adds garbage, and defeats PureComponent-style checks. Bind once in the constructor, or use an arrow field, so the function identity stays stable.

code.title: Arrow functions and this

followUps:
At module top level it is undefined in an ES module and window in a classic browser script, because an arrow just takes the surrounding this. In Node CommonJS it is module.exports (an empty object).

Key point: an object literal is not a scope. So { f: () => this } gives f the file's this, not the object. That is why arrows are poor object methods.

Neither exactly: an arrow has no this of its own, so it looks this up like any other variable in the enclosing scope, at the time it runs. In practice the enclosing function's this is fixed per call, so it behaves as if captured.

function Timer(){
  this.t = 0;
  setInterval(() => this.t++, 1000);
}
// this.t belongs to that Timer instance

Each new Timer() has its own call, so each arrow sees its own this.

code.title: Fixing a detached method

followUps:
Because obj.method as an argument evaluates to just the function; the obj. part is dropped. Later the browser calls the listener with this set to the element, so your own object is not the receiver.

The common bug: el.addEventListener('click', this.onClick.bind(this)) and later el.removeEventListener('click', this.onClick.bind(this)). The second bind makes a different function, so nothing is removed. Store the bound function once and pass that same reference to both calls, or use the signal option.

Prototype methods with one bind per instance are cheapest: shared code, one bound function per instance only where needed. An arrow field makes 10,000 closures per handler, a bound copy makes 10,000 too, and neither is free.

Best of all for big lists: use one listener on the parent (event delegation) and read event.target. That is 1 function instead of 10,000, and it works for rows added later. Memory per closure is roughly 50 to 100 bytes, so 10,000 is about 1 MB per handler.

code.title: new keyword rebuilt by hand

followUps:
function myNew(C, ...args){
  const o = Object.create(C.prototype);
  const r = C.apply(o, args);
  return (r !== null && (typeof r === 'object' || typeof r === 'function')) ? r : o;
}

Steps: make an object linked to C.prototype, run C with this as that object, then return its result if it is an object or function, otherwise the new object. It does not support classes (apply on a class throws); use Reflect.construct for those.

new.target tells you which constructor new was applied to, and it is undefined when the function was called normally. It lets a function detect a missing new.

function P(){
  if (!new.target) return new P();
}
class Base { constructor(){ console.log(new.target.name); } }
class Kid extends Base {}
new Kid(); // 'Kid'

In a parent class it names the actual subclass, which is useful for abstract-class checks.

It throws a TypeError. A derived constructor may only return an object or undefined; returning a primitive like 5 is an error, unlike in a base constructor where primitives are ignored.

class A {}
class B extends A { constructor(){ super(); return 5; } }
new B(); // TypeError: Derived constructors may only return object or undefined

If you return an object instead, that object replaces the instance.

code.title: bind polyfill with new support

followUps:
Before new.target, the polyfill checked this instanceof bound inside the bound function. If true, it was probably called with new, so it used this and ignored thisArg.

function bound(){
  const self = this instanceof bound ? this : thisArg;
  return target.apply(self, preset.concat(args));
}
bound.prototype = Object.create(target.prototype);

It was fragile: it failed with Reflect.construct, subclass newTarget, and it could not construct ES6 classes, because apply on a class throws.

A few: bound functions have no prototype property natively, while a polyfilled normal function has one; the native one also hides the exact internal slots ([[BoundTargetFunction]]). Stack traces and toString() show different text, and it cannot see the engine's internal bound state.

Also Function.prototype.bind.call(nonCallable) messages and property order differ. A normal function's length/name are defined as data, so you must set them with defineProperty, as done above. None of these matter in normal code, but libraries should use native bind.

code.title: Strict mode and this

followUps:
It is the plain global object (globalThis) for a sloppy function, even if the caller is strict. Strictness belongs to the function being called, not the caller.

function sloppy(){ return this === globalThis; }
function strictCaller(){ 'use strict'; return sloppy(); }
strictCaller(); // true

The strict caller passes undefined, and the sloppy callee replaces it with the global object. This is why mixing old and new files can surprise you.

Because the function would then be strict for its parameters too, and the engine needs to know strictness before it evaluates defaults. The spec forbids the directive when the parameter list is not simple (defaults, rest, destructuring), giving a SyntaxError.

function f(a = 1){ 'use strict'; } // SyntaxError

Fix: put 'use strict' at the top of the file or the enclosing function, or use a class or module, which are strict anyway.

code.title: Arrow field vs prototype method

followUps:
Jest's spyOn replaces a property on the object, so it works on prototype methods but only for instances created after you spy on a prototype. An arrow field is an own property created in the constructor, so you must spy on the instance, after it is built.

jest.spyOn(Proto.prototype, 'click'); // works for all instances
const inst = new Field();
jest.spyOn(inst, 'click');            // field: spy on the instance

Spying on Field.prototype.click does nothing because the instance property hides it.

Function components have no this at all. State lives in hooks like useState, and handlers are ordinary closures over the variables of that render.

function Counter(){
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  const inc = () => setN(n + 1);
}

When identity matters (memoized children), useCallback keeps the same function between renders. So the whole this binding problem disappears.

code.title: this in an event listener

followUps:
event.target is the element that started the event (the deepest one clicked); event.currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to, which equals this in a normal function.

Example: a list <ul> with a click listener, and you click an <li>. Then target is the li and currentTarget is the ul. This difference is the basis of event delegation.

You pass one AbortSignal when adding listeners, and calling abort() once removes all of them, with no need to keep each function reference.

const ac = new AbortController();
el.addEventListener('click', onClick, { signal: ac.signal });
win.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal: ac.signal });
ac.abort(); // both removed

It works with arrows and bound functions, which fixes the "cannot remove" bug.

code.title: Top-level this in Node

followUps:
Because in Node every file is wrapped in a function, so a top-level var is a local variable of that function, not a property of the global object. In a browser classic script, a top-level var does become window.x.

var topVar = 1;
console.log(globalThis.topVar); // undefined in Node

let and const never create global properties in either place. ES modules also keep their variables private.

They tested each place in turn: window in browsers, self in workers, global in Node, and used the trick Function('return this')(), which returns the global object even from strict code because functions made this way are sloppy.

const root = typeof self !== 'undefined' ? self
  : typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window
  : typeof global !== 'undefined' ? global : this;

Since ES2020 you just write globalThis.

code.title: Reference record and comma operator

followUps:
Bundlers write (0, mod.fn)() to call an imported function the way the ES spec does: as a plain call with this undefined, not as a method of the module object.

Without the 0,, mod.fn() would pass the module namespace as this. The comma operator turns the reference into a plain value, dropping the object. The result is the same behaviour as import { fn }, where fn() has no receiver.

super.method() looks the method up on the parent's prototype (via the method's [[HomeObject]]) but calls it with the current this, so the instance is the receiver.

class A { who(){ return this.tag; } }
class B extends A {
  tag = 'B';
  who(){ return super.who(); } // 'B'
}

So the parent's code sees the child's fields, which is why overriding works as expected.

code.title: Arrow and bound resist this changes

followUps:
f.bind(a).bind(b) gives a function whose this is still a. The second bind wraps the first bound function, and the first [[BoundThis]] wins.

function f(){ return this.n; }
const g = f.bind({n: 1}).bind({n: 2});
g();      // 1
g.name;   // 'bound bound f'

Extra pre-filled arguments from both calls are combined in order.

No. Bound arrows are not constructors. An arrow has no [[Construct]], and a bound function is only constructible if its target is, so new throws a TypeError.

const b = (() => 1).bind({});
new b(); // TypeError: b is not a constructor

Binding an arrow does nothing useful anyway for this, since the arrow ignores the bound value. It can still pre-fill arguments.

It flags code that pulls a method out of an object and uses it alone, such as const f = obj.method or setTimeout(obj.method), where this would be lost.

class C { n = 1; get(){ return this.n; } }
const c = new C();
const g = c.get; // lint error: unbound-method

It does not complain for arrow-function properties or methods declared with a this: void parameter, because those are safe to detach.

It is the type this inside a class, meaning "whatever subclass this actually is". A method returning this keeps the subclass type when chaining.

class Base { add(n: number): this { return this; } }
class Sub extends Base { extra(): this { return this; } }
new Sub().add(1).extra(); // OK: add returns Sub

If add had returned Base, the call to extra would be a compile error.
